Give the houseplants a drink. Make sure you hydrate often. Avoid listening to the news. Let yourself feel dull and restless. Grumble about the weather. Carry a corkscrew in your handbag. Occasionally swipe right. Only smile if you actually feel like it. Stay in bed late. Don’t watch the news. Keep in mind how the world is arranged for white people. Pay attention to the sound of crickets. Clean between your teeth. Take your medication. Leave your thoughts blank.

If you wake up hungover, don’t announce that you’ll never drink again. Tell the truth when you have the strength for it. If not, drink water, deceive yourself, shut off the news, set the newspapers on fire, avoid the funerals, swallow the pills, laugh at stupid things, sleep with people who mean nothing to you, use the crockpot, use the juicer, use the smoothie machine, drink rainwater, don’t spend too long thinking about the sky, don’t dwell on water, stay away from funerals, and close your eyes whenever you can.

When raising a glass, meet every person’s gaze. Never give the President punctuation. Make the news yourself. Become water. Pour water on the fire escape. Burn the page. Crush the letters. Choose hydrangeas rather than hyacinths. Give the hydrangeas water. Let the news wither. Make the hydrangeas white. Drink the whiteness. Let the cricket songs become a waterfall. Keep your mind full of song. Do not smile. Do not wither. Funeral, funeral.
outputs.L3:
Take care of yourself in the smallest ways you can manage. Drink water. Sleep in when your body asks for it. Floss your teeth even if everything else feels neglected. Take your pills. Water the plants before their leaves begin to curl. These routines may seem too ordinary to matter, but they are a way of remaining connected to life. They are proof that some part of you still believes in tomorrow.

When the world becomes too loud, allow yourself to turn away from it. Turn off the news when it begins to feel like a machine built only to produce dread. Do not force yourself to witness every tragedy in real time. If you cannot attend the funeral, do not go. If you need to sit quietly with an empty mind, let it be empty. Sometimes survival means refusing to look directly at pain until you have the strength to face it.

Be gentle with your imperfect ways of coping. You may be bored. You may make jokes at the wrong time. You may drink too much, or reach for casual intimacy, or tell yourself a lie because the truth feels too heavy to hold. These are not always noble responses, but they are human ones. Exhaustion often makes people strange. Grief can make avoidance feel like shelter. Do not confuse your difficulty with failure.

Pay attention, when you can, to small rituals and sensory details. Listen to the crickets singing in the dark. Raise a glass and make a toast, even if the occasion is unclear. Notice the hum of kitchen appliances, the click of a kettle, the glow of a refrigerator at midnight. Care for flowers, even cut ones, even dying ones. There is meaning in these gestures, not because they solve anything, but because they keep you present.

This way of living is not neat or heroic. It is a mixture of ordinary advice and surreal endurance: flossing beside grief, watering plants while the world burns, making toast under a sky full of impossible noise. The result is a portrait of exhaustion and persistence. It admits the need for avoidance, the ache of loss, and the absurdity of continuing. Still, it insists that continuing is possible, if only through small acts, strange comforts, and the fragile routines that carry us from one day to the next.
outputs.L4:
There are mornings when the world arrives too early. It comes through the phone before the kettle has boiled, through headlines written in the grammar of emergency, through photographs of smoke, floods, hunger, men in suits explaining why cruelty is necessary. It comes through the ceiling, the window, the buzzing light above the bathroom mirror. It comes before you have remembered your own name.

So you develop rituals.

You drink water because someone once told you that despair is worse when dehydrated. You stand at the sink and swallow glass after glass, as if the body were a burning house and this might help. You make coffee. You make it too strong. You make it anyway. You open the curtains, then close them halfway because the light feels accusatory. You water the basil on the windowsill, though the basil has been dying for weeks. You pluck the black leaves off one by one and call this hope.

You do not read the news before breakfast. Then you read the news before breakfast. Then you put the phone face down and promise to become a better person tomorrow.

The day asks things of you. Emails. Passwords. Groceries. A reply to the message you have avoided for three days because it was kind, and kindness requires an answer you are not sure you can give. There are forms to fill out. There are appointments to make. There is laundry in the machine that has soured because you forgot it yesterday. You run it again. You add detergent. You add vinegar. You believe, briefly, in cleansing.

Outside, everything continues.

A minister lies on television. A river catches fire. Someone says “collateral damage” with a clean mouth. Someone says “economic reality.” Someone says “we are all in this together” from a room no one you know could afford to enter. The planet warms. The rent rises. The group chat sends a meme of a raccoon standing in a trash can with the caption, it me. You laugh so hard you make a small, ugly sound. The laughter embarrasses you. Then it saves you for seven minutes.

You begin keeping lists.

Things to do:
- Buy soap.
- Call the dentist.
- Stop imagining the end of everything while brushing teeth.
- Take out recycling.
- Become less afraid.
- Defrost soup.
- Answer one email.
- Do not become a stone.
- Do not become a screen.
- Do not become your mother’s silence.
- Buy more soap.

The lists help because they break the impossible into pieces small enough to carry. Not solve. Carry. There is a difference. You cannot end the war before noon, but you can put clean sheets on the bed. You cannot undo the election, the oil spill, the algorithm, the old grief lodged under the ribs, but you can cut an onion. You can heat a pan. You can feed yourself something warm and say, even if you do not believe it, here, stay.

Sometimes survival looks embarrassingly domestic. A folded towel. A charged phone. A banana eaten over the sink. Sometimes it looks like not answering. Sometimes it looks like answering with a single heart emoji because language has become too heavy. Sometimes it looks like putting on shoes and walking around the block while the mind narrates catastrophe in a calm, documentary voice.

On the worst days, you practice avoidance with the devotion of a monk.

You watch videos of people restoring old furniture. You watch a woman make a miniature lasagna for a hamster. You watch a man remove rust from a knife until the blade shines like a recovered moon. You watch strangers organize pantries into transparent containers labeled flour, rice, sugar, oats, as if naming were a form of control. You watch rain fall in cities you have never visited. You watch a livestream of jellyfish pulsing blue in an aquarium tank, going nowhere beautifully.

You tell yourself this is not living. Then you tell yourself it is not dying either.

There are small pleasures, and you learn not to despise them. The first sip of coffee. The smell of oranges under your thumbnail. The private luxury of cancelling plans. A dog leaning its whole body against your shin at a crosswalk. Clean socks. Butter melting into toast. The moment in a song when the drums arrive. A stranger’s baby waving at you from a bus. The word “coriander.” The moon appearing above a petrol station, indifferent and theatrical.

You collect these things like coins from a country that may no longer exist.

At night, the body becomes strange. Your hands look borrowed. Your face in the dark window seems to belong to someone waiting outside. You lie in bed and feel yourself transforming. Not dramatically, not into anything useful like a bird or a storm, but into minor, inconvenient shapes. A drawer full of dead batteries. A moth in a lampshade. A spoon left in the freezer. A houseplant turning toward artificial light.

Sometimes you become fog. Sometimes you become a small black dog hiding under a table during fireworks. Sometimes you become an entire city at 4 a.m., all locked doors and humming refrigerators. Sometimes you become your own childhood bedroom, where the wallpaper is peeling and something is breathing in the closet. Sometimes you become the closet.

In the morning, you become a person again because the alarm insists.

You learn to perform personhood by repetition. Wash face. Brush teeth. Apply moisturizer. Put one foot into one pant leg, then the other. Check pockets for keys. Stand in the doorway. Return for the keys. Leave. Re-enter. Turn off the stove you did not turn on. Leave again.

The repetition is not glamorous. It does not heal the wound; it keeps the wound from becoming the whole body. It is a line of stones across a flooded field. It is not a bridge, exactly, but it gives the foot somewhere to land.

People say, “How are you?” and you become a skilled editor.

“Fine,” you say.

“Busy,” you say.

“Hanging in there,” you say, which is the most honest phrase available, because it contains both the noose and the branch.

With close friends, you become more precise. “I am full of wet cement.” “I am a haunted vending machine.” “I am trying not to read comments under anything.” “I cried because the supermarket stopped carrying the good noodles.” They understand. They send back pictures of their cats, their lunches, their own faces under fluorescent office light. Proof of life. Proof of absurdity. Proof that everyone is still here, or trying to be.

Humor becomes a hinge. Without it, the door will not open.

You joke about the apocalypse because the apocalypse does not have the courtesy to remain metaphorical. You joke about your nervous system like it is a problematic roommate. You joke about capitalism, therapy, back pain, the suspicious optimism of people who wake up at five to jog. You joke because seriousness alone would calcify you. You joke because the powerful prefer your fear pure and uninterrupted. You joke because the laugh, however brief, returns your body to you.

Still, there are limits. There are days when no ritual works. The coffee is bitter. The basil is dead. The laundry smells wrong. The phone glows like a portal to punishment. On those days, you lower the standard. You do not aim for joy. You do not aim for productivity, enlightenment, resistance, transformation, closure. You aim for maintenance.

Eat something.

Stand up.

Open a window.

Take the medication.

Send the message: “I’m not doing great, but I’m here.”

Let someone send back: “I’m here too.”

That may be all. That may be enormous.

There is no final resolution. The world does not become gentle because you bought fresh lemons or cleaned the bathroom sink. The machinery does not stop because you took a nap. Grief is not defeated by soup. Fascism is not frightened by your skincare routine. The seas will not cool because you remembered to stretch.

And yet.

The lemon brightens the room. The sink shines. The nap makes tomorrow slightly more possible. The soup enters the body and becomes heat. The stretched muscle loosens its grip on pain. These things do not fix the world. They keep you from abandoning it completely.

Perhaps survival is not a single brave act but a series of ordinary refusals: refusing to disappear, refusing to become only numb, refusing to let horror have every room in the house. You make the bed not because everything is fine, but because everything is not. You sweep the floor because dust accumulates even during empire. You sing while washing dishes because the body remembers rhythm before it remembers despair.

And when the world arrives again, as it always does, too loud and too early, you meet it imperfectly. You drink water. You curse. You laugh at the raccoon in the trash can. You water what is dying. You throw away what cannot be saved. You begin the list again.
outputs.L5:
Don always believed that the simplest habits could make the biggest difference. Every morning, before coffee or breakfast, he would drink a glass of water. It helped him feel awake, refreshed, and ready for the day.

Water is one of the most important things our bodies need. It keeps us healthy, supports our energy, and helps us stay focused. Don often reminded his friends to carry a bottle of water with them, especially on hot days or after exercise.

For Don, choosing to drink water was not just a habit—it was a small way to take care of himself every day.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem made of imperative life advice, starting with “Water the plants” and “Drink plenty of water,” gradually dissolving into repetition, news avoidance, flowers, drinking, and fragmented language.
counterfactuals.output:
Water the plants.  
Drink plenty of water,  
then apologize to the windows for all they have seen.

Keep a bowl of lemons near the door.  
Sleep when the moon forgets your name.  
Fold your shirts as if they are small, exhausted flags.  
Do not argue with mirrors after midnight.  
Leave bread for the invisible birds.

Avoid the news today.  
Avoid the news tomorrow.  
Avoid the news until the news grows moss,  
until it knocks softly and asks to be a flower.  
Say no.  
Say bloom.  
Say nothing.

Water the plants again.  
Drink plenty of water.  
Water the water.  
Plant the drink.  
Let the flowers open their red mouths  
and tell you what not to know.

Do not read the burning headline.  
Do not sip the sirens.  
Do not refresh the thunder.  
Refresh the glass.  
Refresh the vase.  
Refresh the throat full of petals.

Drink.  
Drink carefully.  
Drink from the blue cup.  
Drink from the cloud.  
Drink what the roses have forgotten.  
Water the plants.  
Water the plants.  
Water the plants until the room becomes a garden  
and the garden becomes a sentence  
and the sentence loses its shoes.

Avoid.  
Avoid the news.  
Avoid the new.  
Avoid the knew.  
No knowing before breakfast.  
No breakfast before lilies.  
No lilies without rain.

Flower the table.  
Flower the mouth.  
Flower the wound in the radio.  
Turn it off.  
Turn off the voice that counts the fires.  
Turn off the fire that counts your hands.  
Turn.  
Off.  
Turn.

Drink plenty.  
Drink plants.  
Plant plenty.  
Plenty the water.  
Water water water  
the plants the plants the plants  
the glass grass green grief  
sip sip stem

Do not—  
do not read—  
do not read the—  

Rose.  
Rose.  
Rosewater.

Drink.

Water the.

Plants.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental second-person poem in the style of a list of instructions for surviving modern life, with motifs of water, plants, the news, funerals, pills, and emotional numbness.
counterfactuals.output:
**Instructions for Continuing**

1. Wake before the news can name you.  
   Do not look directly at the screen.  
   Let the anchors pour their black water  
   into the room without drinking.

2. Keep a plant on the windowsill.  
   Call it evidence.  
   When its leaves yellow, apologize  
   with the sincerity you reserve for funerals.

3. Swallow the pill with a full glass of water.  
   Swallow the water with a full glass of silence.  
   If you feel nothing, mark this as improvement.  
   If you feel too much, mark this as weather.

4. Practice your face in the mirror:  
   concerned for the burning city,  
   grateful for the email,  
   composed beside the open casket,  
   alive but not insisting on it.

5. When someone asks how you are,  
   become a houseplant.  
   Require light.  
   Mention neither the soil nor the worms.

6. At the funeral, touch the lilies only if necessary.  
   Their white mouths are not answers.  
   Stand where the rain can find you.  
   Let it prove your body is still a body.

7. Read the headlines in small doses.  
   Flood. Fire. War. Recall. Shortage.  
   Say each word like a tablet on the tongue.  
   Do not chew.

8. If grief arrives, offer it a chair  
   but not the remote.  
   If joy arrives, suspect a clerical error.  
   If numbness arrives, let it wear your coat  
   and answer your messages.

9. Water the plant on Thursdays.  
   Water yourself whenever you remember  
   you are mostly water  
   pretending to be a calendar.

10. Do not confuse survival with healing.  
    Survival is the plastic fern in the waiting room.  
    Healing is harder to identify  
    and often dies when overhandled.

11. Keep a spare pill in your bag.  
    Keep a spare condolence in your mouth.  
    Keep a spare version of yourself  
    for people who loved you before the news.

12. When the world ends, it will likely be incremental:  
    a notification, a drought,  
    a nurse drawing the curtain,  
    the basil wilting overnight.

13. Still, rinse the cup.  
    Still, open the blinds.  
    Still, press your thumb into the soil  
    to see what thirst remains.

14. If you cannot cry, run the faucet.  
    If you cannot pray, mist the leaves.  
    If you cannot feel, stand in the rain  
    until the rain feels you.

15. Repeat after no one:  
    you are not required to bloom.  
    you are not required to be useful.  
    you are not required to turn pain  
    into a garden.

16. But if something green insists  
    on rising through the crack,  
    do not call it hope too quickly.  
    Give it water.  
    Give it room.  
    Let it frighten you  
    by living.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness list poem that begins like practical self-care advice but becomes increasingly chaotic and poetic, repeating words like water, news, hydrangeas, and funeral.
counterfactuals.output:
Drink water before you read the news.  
Stretch your neck. Unclench your jaw.  
Put the kettle on.  
Open a window if the room has become a room  
inside your chest.  

Call someone back.  
Do not call everyone back.  
Buy hydrangeas if they are on sale,  
or just look at hydrangeas  
through the florist glass, blue as weather,  
pink as an apology.  

Eat something with a name you trust.  
Toast. Soup. Apple.  
Water. More water.  
The news can wait.  
The news is waiting anyway,  
panting softly in the hallway  
with its mouth full of wires.  

Fold the blanket.  
Do not fold yourself.  
Stand in sunlight for seven minutes.  
Say funeral once,  
then say it again more gently: funeral,  
as if it were a boat you could push  
from the shore without climbing in.  

Water the hydrangeas.  
Water the basil.  
Water the idea of tomorrow  
until it grows strange leaves.  
The news says rain.  
The news says fire.  
The news says funeral, funeral, funeral,  
but the hydrangeas keep making  
their ridiculous blue fists.  

Breathe in for four.  
Hold for four.  
Forget what number means.  
A spoon in the sink becomes a moon,  
the moon becomes a headline,  
the headline becomes water,  
water becomes a voice saying  
not yet, not yet, not yet.  

Take a walk around the block.  
If the block is gone, walk around the memory of it.  
If memory is gone, follow the hydrangeas.  
They know where the funeral hid the music.  
They know where the news buried the birds.  
They know the password is water  
and the door is also water  
and you are knocking from inside the water.  

Do not doomscroll after midnight.  
Do not midnight after doom.  
Do not funeral the hydrangeas  
unless they ask you to.  
Do not news the water  
unless the water is already screaming.  
Do not scream unless you must,  
and then scream into a clean towel,  
a clean sky,  
a clean animal of air.  

Remember: breakfast.  
Remember: socks.  
Remember: the small pill, the green mug,  
the name of the street where you once felt forgiven.  
Remember water, news, hydrangeas, funeral.  
Water, news, hydrangeas, funeral.  
Water news hydrangeas funeral.  
Waternews. Hydrangeafuneral.  
Blue mouth. Wet paper.  
A bell made of petals.  
A casket full of rain.  

And if you wake tomorrow  
with the news in your hair  
and the funeral under your tongue  
and hydrangeas blooming from every faucet,  
drink water.  
Drink water.  
Drink the bright unbearable water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly funny feminist advice poem about coping, drinking, politics, dating apps, weather, and despair, using commands and ending in surreal wordplay.
counterfactuals.output:
Drink water between disasters.  
Call your senator, then call him a cab.  
Delete the app that thinks “moderate” is a personality.  
Swipe left on men holding fish,  
men holding grudges,  
men holding forth about “biological destiny”  
from a mattress on the floor.

Carry pepper spray and lip gloss.  
Carry snacks.  
Carry the generational rage  
in a tote bag that says LOCAL BOOKSTORE.  
Do not apologize when it hits someone.

Check the weather.  
If it says “chance of men,” bring an umbrella.  
If it says “unseasonably warm,” blame capitalism.  
If it hails, name each stone after a Supreme Court justice  
and let the sky finish the argument.

Vote while exhausted.  
Laugh while doomed.  
Moisturize against the void.  
Text your friends: Are you alive?  
Accept replies like: Physically, yes.  
Make soup. Make noise.  
Make rent somehow.  
Make eye contact with the moon  
until she admits she’s tired too.

When despair climbs into bed wearing your ex’s hoodie,  
tell it: Shoes off in this house.  
When hope arrives late and drunk,  
let her in anyway.  
Give her the couch.  
Hide the good gin.

Date if you must,  
but keep your standards sharp enough  
to cut a headline in half.  
Kiss only those who understand  
that feminism is not a debate topic  
but the reason they still have teeth.

And when the world ends,  
arrive overdressed.  
Bring a flask, a ballot, and a cardigan.  
Stand in the ash and announce:  
Ladies, we are not spiraling—  
we are merely becoming weatherwise,  
whether-wise,  
witherwise,  
witcherwise,  
a coven of umbrellas blooming in the doom-room broom-gloom.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an avant-garde poem composed mostly of imperative sentences, mixing mundane habits like flossing and using a crockpot with dreamlike images of fire escapes, cricket songs, white hydrangeas, and wilting news.
counterfactuals.output:
Floss before the moon files its teeth.  
Load the crockpot with onions, rainwater, and a small apology.  
Set it to low.  
Let the apartment learn patience.

Climb the fire escape backward.  
Count every rung as a vanished address.  
Listen for cricket songs in the radiator.  
Answer them with your wrists.

Rinse the spoon.  
Fold the towels into obedient weather.  
Press your ear to the white hydrangeas.  
Tell them not to bloom so loudly.

Unplug the lamp.  
Peel yesterday’s headline from the window.  
Do not trust the wilting news.  
Bury it under coffee grounds.

Scrub the sink until it remembers the ocean.  
Leave one dish for the ghosts.  
Stir the stew clockwise.  
Dream counterclockwise.

Open the door without entering.  
Hang your coat on a flame.  
Teach the smoke your childhood name.  
Floss again, gently, between the stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
